comparisons.peer_summary: AMD relies on patents, copyrights, and trade secrets to protect its technology but cannot assure adequate protection from infringement or misappropriation. Risks include patent applications failing to issue or being issued in disadvantageous forms, independent development of similar products by competitors, and difficulties in enforcing intellectual property rights in jurisdictions with weaker legal protections.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVDA and AMD rely on a combination of patents, trademarks, trade secrets, and contractual agreements to protect their intellectual property, yet both acknowledge that these measures may not be sufficient to prevent infringement or misappropriation, particularly in foreign jurisdictions where legal protections are weaker. NVDA specifically highlights the risk of trade secret theft harming competitive position, while AMD explicitly warns that inadequate protection could lead to lost competitive advantage and significant expenses.

sentences.text: We rely on patents, trademarks, trade secrets, employee and third-party nondisclosure agreements, licensing arrangements and the laws of the countries in which we operate to protect our IP.
Foreign laws may not protect our products or IP rights to the same extent as United States law.

The theft or unauthorized use or publication of our trade secrets and other confidential information could harm our competitive position and reduce acceptance of our products; as a result, the value of our investment in research and development, product development and marketing could be reduced.

If we cannot adequately protect our technology or other intellectual property in the United States and abroad, through patents, copyrights, trade secrets, trademarks and other measures, we may lose a competitive advantage and incur significant expenses.

However, we cannot assure you that we will be able to adequately protect our technology or other intellectual property from third-party infringement or from misappropriation in the United States and abroad.

In jurisdictions where foreign laws provide less intellectual property protection than afforded in the U.S. and abroad, our technology or other intellectual property may be compromised, and our business would be materially adversely affected.

comparisons.peer_summary: The company's success depends on protecting IP through patents, copyrights, and trademarks; failure to protect IP or limited protection in jurisdictions could harm the business. Licensing obligations from acquisitions or exclusive licenses may limit the ability to assert IP rights, and inability to obtain or renew necessary IP licenses could materially adversely affect operations.
comparisons.comparison: NVDA and AVGO both disclose reliance on patents, copyrights, trademarks, and trade secrets to protect IP, while acknowledging the risk that failure to adequately protect these rights could adversely affect their business. NVDA focuses on the uncertainty of formal protection approvals and enforceability, whereas AVGO emphasizes the significant resources spent monitoring IP and the risk that even with such expenditures, valuable IP rights may not be sufficiently protected.

sentences.text: We rely on patents, trademarks, trade secrets, employee and third-party nondisclosure agreements, licensing arrangements and the laws of the countries in which we operate to protect our IP.

We continuously assess whether and where to seek formal protection for existing and new innovations and technologies but cannot be certain whether our applications for such protections will be approved, and, if approved, whether they will be enforceable.
If we are unable or fail to protect our IP, our business could be adversely affected.

To accomplish this, we rely on a combination of IP rights, including patents, copyrights, trademarks and trade secrets, as well as customary contractual protections with our customers, suppliers, employees and consultants.
Even with significant expenditures, we may not be able to protect the IP rights that are valuable to our business or have sufficient IP rights to protect our products or our business.

comparisons.peer_topic: Intellectual Property Protection and Enforcement Risks
comparisons.peer_summary: Intel faces risks in protecting and enforcing its IP rights due to litigation, varying enforceability, and geopolitical factors, including compulsory licensing. Additionally, licensing practices and industry standard participation may allow competitors to use patents or exhaust rights, impairing IP value.
comparisons.comparison: NVDA and INTC share specific language regarding the risk that theft or unauthorized use of trade secrets and confidential information could harm their competitive position and reduce the value of their R&D and marketing investments. Both companies also acknowledge the limitations of IP protection mechanisms, with NVDA noting uncertainty regarding approval/enforceability and INTC stating it cannot always protect or enforce its IP rights.

sentences.text: The theft or unauthorized use or publication of our trade secrets and other confidential information could harm our competitive position and reduce acceptance of our products; as a result, the value of our investment in research and development, product development and marketing could be reduced.

We continuously assess whether and where to seek formal protection for existing and new innovations and technologies but cannot be certain whether our applications for such protections will be approved, and, if approved, whether they will be enforceable.
We cannot always protect our IP or enforce our IP rights.
We rely on IP law-as well as confidentiality and licensing agreements with our customers, employees, technology development partners, and others-to protect our IP and IP rights.

In addition, the theft or unauthorized use or publication of our trade secrets and other confidential business information could harm our competitive position and reduce acceptance of our products; as a result, the value of our investment in R&D, product development, and marketing could be reduced.

comparisons.peer_topic: Intellectual Property Protection Risks and AI Impact
comparisons.peer_summary: The company maintains a system of controls over its intellectual property, but competitors may still illegally obtain or disclose proprietary information, especially with laws in some foreign countries offering weaker protection. The use of AI in product development could also lead to IP loss or infringement risks.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVDA and MU highlight the risk that foreign laws may not protect intellectual property to the same extent as U.S. laws, increasing the potential for piracy or unauthorized use. NVDA specifically mentions that foreign laws may not protect IP rights to the same extent, while MU states that laws in some foreign countries may not protect IP to the same degree and that confidentiality agreements may be difficult to enforce in those jurisdictions.

sentences.text: Foreign laws may not protect our products or IP rights to the same extent as United States law.

Despite our system of controls over our intellectual property, it may be possible for our current or future competitors to obtain, copy, use, or disclose, illegally or otherwise, our product and process technology or other proprietary information.

The laws of some foreign countries may not protect our intellectual property to the same degree as do U.S. laws, and our confidentiality, non-disclosure, and non-compete agreements may be unenforceable or difficult and costly to enforce.

comparisons.peer_topic: Risks of foreign IP law variations and policy changes
comparisons.peer_summary: Laws in certain foreign countries may not protect Qualcomm's intellectual property rights to the same extent as U.S. laws, and there is uncertainty regarding future changes in laws, policies, or practices of standards bodies that could be detrimental to licensing programs or product sales.
comparisons.comparison: NVDA and QCOM both explicitly disclose that intellectual property laws in certain foreign countries do not protect IP rights to the same extent as United States laws. NVDA notes this increases piracy risks, while QCOM adds uncertainty about future changes in foreign laws and standards body practices that could be detrimental to licensing programs.

sentences.text: Foreign laws may not protect our products or IP rights to the same extent as United States law.

Further, the laws in certain foreign countries in which our patents are or may be licensed, or our products are or may be manufactured or sold, including certain countries in Asia, may not protect our intellectual property rights to the same extent as the laws in the United States.

comparisons.peer_topic: Risks of IP protection and enforcement costs
comparisons.peer_summary: The enforcement and protection of Qualcomm's intellectual property may be expensive, ineffective in preventing misappropriation, or adversely affected by changes in patent laws and ineffective enforcement in foreign jurisdictions. The company relies on various legal mechanisms and agreements, but policing unauthorized use is difficult, and past steps have not always prevented misappropriation, particularly in countries with weaker laws.
comparisons.comparison: NVDA and QCOM both recognize that relying on patent, trademark, trade secret, and confidentiality agreements does not guarantee protection against misappropriation, particularly in foreign jurisdictions. NVDA cites the risk of employees being hired by competitors and the uncertainty of enforcement, while QCOM emphasizes that policing unauthorized use is difficult and that past steps have not always prevented misappropriation in countries with weaker laws.

sentences.text: We rely on patents, trademarks, trade secrets, employee and third-party nondisclosure agreements, licensing arrangements and the laws of the countries in which we operate to protect our IP.
We also may face risks to our IP if our employees are hired by competitors.

We continuously assess whether and where to seek formal protection for existing and new innovations and technologies but cannot be certain whether our applications for such protections will be approved, and, if approved, whether they will be enforceable.

The enforcement and protection of our intellectual property may be expensive, could fail to prevent misappropriation or unauthorized use of our intellectual property, could result in the loss of our ability to enforce one or more patents, and could be adversely affected by changes in patent laws, by laws in certain foreign jurisdictions that may not effectively protect our intellectual property and by ineffective enforcement of laws in such jurisdictions.

We rely primarily on patent, copyright, trademark and trade secret laws, as well as nondisclosure and confidentiality agreements, international treaties and other methods, to protect our intellectual property, including our patent portfolio.

The steps we have taken have not always prevented, and we cannot be certain the steps we take in the future will prevent, the misappropriation or unauthorized use of our products, technologies or intellectual property, particularly in foreign countries where the laws may not protect our rights as fully or as readily as U.S. laws or where the enforcement of such laws may be lacking or ineffective.
